title: Mazhabi Sikhs
hookLine: Sikhs from Dalit backgrounds, heirs of Bhai Jaita, who served in honored regiments

lines: A BUNDLE CARRIED OUT OF DELHI.
THE HEAD OF GURU TEGH BAHADUR.
BHAI JAITA, COUNTED AMONG THE LOWEST.
cards: A man walks out of Delhi at night with a bundle held close against his chest. He keeps off the main roads; every checkpoint is a danger. What he carries is the head of Guru Tegh Bahadur, executed in the city.

He is taking it to the Guru's young son, far to the north. Two days ago we followed the trader who carried the Guru's body home; this is the other road out of Delhi. His name, in Sikh memory, is Bhai Jaita.
He came from a family that the society around him counted among the lowest. Today we meet the Sikhs who call him their own.

teach.b: Mazhabi Sikhs are Sikhs from Dalit backgrounds, from communities the caste order pushed to its bottom rung. In the panth they honor Bhai Jaita as their forebear.

As tradition tells it, Bhai Jaita reached Anandpur and laid the Guru's head before the young Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru embraced him and spoke a phrase Sikhs still repeat: the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons.
Rangreta is a name tradition uses for Bhai Jaita's people. In a single sentence, a community the world treated as outcast was claimed as family by the Guru himself.
Tradition remembers Bhai Jaita later taking amrit and fighting beside the Guru.
Mazhabi Sikhs carried that courage into later centuries, serving in regiments of the army known for their battle honors, a point of deep pride. The story has a harder side.
The Gurus' teaching on caste is plain, but caste prejudice has not vanished among Sikhs any more than among others. In places, Mazhabi Sikhs have faced exclusion, even in matters of worship.
Sikh voices have long spoken against that, citing the Gurus.

teach.h: ANG 349: SEE THE LIGHT, NOT THE CASTE.
teach.b: One of those lines: Guru Nanak, in Raag Asa on Ang 349, says in paraphrase: recognize the light in each person, and don't ask about caste; in what lies ahead, there is no caste.
The Guru's embrace at Anandpur was that line lived out. The man carrying the Guru's head through the dark was family.
The phrase the Guru's own sons isn't a compliment; it's a claim the panth is still asked to live up to.

how: Mazhabi Sikhs remember Bhai Jaita, who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head to Anandpur, and the saying that the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons; they take pride in their service in the army's honored regiments.

games.q: you're the young Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur. Bhai Jaita, from a people counted lowest, lays your father's head before you. what do you do?
o: reward him with money and send him home.
embrace him and call his people the Guru's own sons.
games.why: tradition says the Guru embraced him and spoke the phrase Sikhs still repeat: the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons.

practice: Settle into a few slow breaths, and let someone come to mind whose work or worth goes unseen: a person on the night shift, someone never invited to the front.
Breathe in and see the light in them, plainly, without a label; breathe out and hold their name as you would a family member's.
